verdicts.trueWording: spinning its Rolodex of 20-30 generic images, selecting one at random
verdicts.note: Raw tumblr HTML fetched with browser UA (200, post dated 2025-03-15 00:18 GMT). Quoted point 3 of Coagulopath's 7-point description, reproduced verbatim by nostalgebraist: 'an overwhelmingly reliance on cliche. Everything is a shadow, an echo, a whisper, a void, a heartbeat, a pulse, a river, a flower-you see it spinning its Rolodex of 20-30 generic images and selecting one at random.' Attribution limb ('Here's a selection from Coagulopath's 7-point description of R1's style in that comment') supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Every line of dialog advances the plot; nothing has weight
verdicts.note: Same raw page. Quoted point 5: 'an eyeball-flatteningly fast pace... Every line of dialog advances the plot. Every description is functional. Nothing is allowed to exist, or to breathe... Nothing on the page has any weight or heft.' Every limb (dialogue advances plot, description functional, nothing has weight) is on the page verbatim; note the source spelling is 'dialog'.

verdicts.trueWording: almost pointless reprompting it: you just get the same stuff again
verdicts.note: Same raw page. Quoted point 7: 'The way how, if you don't like a story, it's almost pointless reprompting it: you just get the same stuff again, smeared around your plate a bit.' Both limbs (reprompting after a disliked story; almost pointless) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Sentences are roughly the same length. The cadence never varies.
verdicts.note: Raw Substack HTML fetched (200, byline 'Charlie Guo, Oct 22, 2025'). Section 'Monotony': 'AI-generated content often has a repetitive structure. Sentences are roughly the same length. Paragraphs follow the same rhythm. The cadence never varies.' Both limbs verbatim; the section sits inside the article's tells (under 'Structural Patterns'), so 'lists monotony as a tell' holds.

verdicts.trueWording: uncommon to see LLMs switch person; they pick a lane
verdicts.note: Same raw page, 'Monotony': 'Creative writing varies not only sentence structure, but also tense and point of view. It's uncommon to see LLMs switch from second or third person to first, and vice versa. They tend to pick a lane and stay in it with unnatural consistency.' Quote verbatim. The 'person' limb is explicit; 'tense' is named one sentence earlier as the axis creative writing varies and is carried by 'pick a lane', so the whole claim stands, though the LLM-specific sentence itself names only person.

verdicts.trueWording: AI metaphors are... plausible. Generic. Human ones specific or resonant.
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'Awkward Analogies': 'Human metaphors tend to be either highly specific (drawing from personal experience) or culturally resonant (drawing from shared references). AI metaphors are... plausible. Generic. They gesture toward meaning without quite achieving it.' All three limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: That specific combination - surface polish with nothing underneath - is AI's signature
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'Filler': 'That specific combination - surface polish with nothing underneath - is AI's signature.' Quote verbatim. The page word is 'signature'; the claim's 'signature failure' is supported by the surrounding framing ('Maybe the biggest red flag' / prose that 'looks and sounds correct until it's put under scrutiny').

verdicts.trueWording: a paragraph said in four sentences what one could say
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'Filler': 'I'll realize that a paragraph has said in four sentences something that could easily have been said in one. The other three sentences added zero to the piece - if anything, they distracted from the point.' All limbs verbatim, including the 'other three adding nothing' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: Perfect grammar is no longer the smoking gun it once was
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'The Red Herrings', bullet 'Typos (or lack thereof)': 'With tools like Grammarly becoming more prevalent... a lack of typos may mean the text went through spell check, not that it was entirely generated by AI. Perfect grammar is no longer the smoking gun it once was.' Quote verbatim; 'rejects as a tell' matches the section's framing ('Before we discuss the reliable tells, let's address a couple of red herrings... I don't think any of them should be considered conclusive'), though Guo also calls them 'yellow flags - worth noticing'.

verdicts.trueWording: good writer uses these devices sparingly, and with intention; AI litters
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'Pattern Matching': 'The main difference is that a good writer uses these devices sparingly, and with intention... AI litters them throughout its writing indiscriminately.' Preceded by 'human writers (even good ones!) use these patterns too', which supports the 'devices themselves are not the difference' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: AI writing detectors don't work. They produce false positives at alarming rates
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'Pattern Matching': 'so-called "AI writing detectors" don't work. They produce false positives at alarming rates, flagging human-written content as AI-generated based on crude heuristics.' Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: cultivate specificity... things AI still struggles to replicate convincingly
verdicts.note: Same raw page, closing section 'Articulate Architecture': 'my own defense against AI slop isn't to worry too much about style and structure. It's to cultivate specificity: to write things rooted in particular knowledge and tangible experience... These are things that AI still struggles to replicate convincingly.' All limbs verbatim; the page's 'These are things' covers specificity plus voice and point of view.

verdicts.trueWording: GPT-4o does this more than its predecessors (anecdotally, more than GPT-5)
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'Lists (And Emojis)': 'I've noticed that GPT-4o does this more than its predecessors (and anecdotally, more than GPT-5). It's rare for me to see Claude do it, though that may be biased by my system prompts.' 'this' refers to emoji-led bullet lists in professional contexts, matching the claim. All three limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: all these generated stories are kinda trash
verdicts.note: Raw WordPress HTML fetched (200), 'Posted on February 23, 2023'. Opening paragraph: 'Technically yes, as this New York Times story about people flooding science fiction magazines with AI-generated story submissions makes evident. But realistically, no, because all these generated stories are kinda trash...' Date and flooding limbs both supported (Scalzi attributes the flooding to scamsters using AI, which the claim does not contradict).

verdicts.trueWording: an editor will see the current AI tropes dozens of times
verdicts.note: Same raw page, paragraph beginning 'If this is indeed mostly scamsters': 'if you're prompting an AI to vomit out text, that one exposure you have to it might make it seem like it's generated something sufficiently original, especially if you otherwise know very little about the genre. But if you're an editor, you'll see the current AI tropes dozens of times with each new iteration.' Same paragraph supplies 'each new iteration of AI text generators'. All limbs verbatim.
